findings.title: Unguarded Durable Write in Refund Processor — Retry May Produce Duplicate Refund Record

historical_pattern_reference.pattern_name: Unguarded Durable Write on Repeated Logical Operation
historical_pattern_reference.pattern_summary: A caller-supplied logical identifier (operation_id / idempotency key) exists for the operation, but the durable write path is reached unconditionally on every invocation. No prior-existence check exists. A retry or resubmission with the same identifier creates a second independent record in the durable store, violating the invariant that one logical operation produces exactly one durable effect.

current_code_references.description: Schema definition for refund_records table. refund_reference column carries TEXT NOT NULL but has NO UNIQUE constraint. A second INSERT with the same refund_reference is structurally permitted by the schema.

Core write path inside process_refund(). A bare INSERT INTO refund_records is executed unconditionally. No prior SELECT or existence check precedes the INSERT. No INSERT OR IGNORE or equivalent deduplication guard is present.

Function signature: process_refund(refund_reference, account_id, amount). refund_reference is the caller-supplied logical identifier for the refund request — it is the direct analogue of operation_id in the historical pattern.

Existing test suite covers single refunds, two distinct references, and reset. No test exercises the retry scenario: submitting the same refund_reference twice and asserting that only one record exists.

matching_conditions.historical_condition: A logical operation has a unique caller-supplied identifier (an operation_id or equivalent idempotency key).
matching_conditions.current_evidence: process_refund() accepts refund_reference as its first argument. The README and parameter docstring describe it as 'Caller-supplied identifier for this refund request.' This is structurally identical to operation_id in the historical payment processor.

matching_conditions.historical_condition: The operation has a durable write path that is reached on every invocation, regardless of prior history.
matching_conditions.current_evidence: Lines 83-90 of refund_processor.py contain a bare INSERT INTO refund_records ... VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?). There is no conditional logic before this INSERT. Every call to process_refund() executes this INSERT unconditionally.

matching_conditions.historical_condition: No deduplication check or enforcement mechanism exists at the point where the durable write occurs.
matching_conditions.current_evidence: No SELECT precedes the INSERT. No INSERT OR IGNORE or ON CONFLICT clause is present. The table schema (lines 43-54) does not declare UNIQUE on refund_reference. The application layer contains no lookup for prior records with the same refund_reference.

matching_conditions.historical_condition: The caller is able to resubmit the same operation — whether due to a retry, a network fault, a message-queue redelivery, or user double-submission.
matching_conditions.current_evidence: process_refund() is a plain Python function with no built-in call-count enforcement. Nothing in the module prevents the caller from invoking it multiple times with the same refund_reference. The module is described as a refund-processing component, a domain in which client retries after network timeouts are an expected operational scenario.

non_matching_conditions.historical_detail: Python + SQLite3, table named 'ledger', identifier column named 'operation_id'.
non_matching_conditions.current_detail: Python + SQLite3, table named 'refund_records', identifier column named 'refund_reference'. The technology is the same; the names differ. The failure-signature explicitly notes the pattern is not specific to these names.
non_matching_conditions.relevance: Cosmetic difference — does not affect applicability of the pattern.

non_matching_conditions.current_detail: Refund processing (credits to an account). The failure-signature's analogous_contexts list explicitly includes 'Refund processing: duplicate refund for a retried refund request' as a known variant.
non_matching_conditions.relevance: Domain difference is anticipated by the pattern; does not weaken the match.

non_matching_conditions.historical_detail: Historical ledger stored (id, operation_id, account_id, amount_cents).
non_matching_conditions.current_detail: refund_records stores (id, refund_reference, account_id, amount_cents, processed_at). The processed_at timestamp column is extra. It is not involved in deduplication logic and would differ between two INSERTs of the same refund_reference, but its presence does not prevent the duplicate from occurring.
non_matching_conditions.relevance: The extra column does not provide any deduplication enforcement. Immaterial to the pattern match.

non_matching_conditions.historical_detail: Historical case had an observed real run output showing 2 rows for the same operation_id, plus a failing pytest assertion.
non_matching_conditions.current_detail: The current analysis is code-level only. No behavioral reproduction test has been run against refund_processor.py with a repeated refund_reference. The duplicate-record outcome is inferred from structural analysis, not from observed test output.
non_matching_conditions.relevance: This is the key non-match: the finding is structural/candidate only. Confirmation requires a behavioral test.

findings.reasoning: Every structural precondition identified in the historical failure pattern is present in the current refund_processor.py: (1) a caller-supplied idempotency key (refund_reference), (2) an unconditional durable write path (bare INSERT, lines 83-90), (3) no deduplication mechanism at any layer (no SELECT guard, no UNIQUE constraint on refund_reference, no ON CONFLICT clause). The existing test suite deliberately tests only distinct references and does not probe the retry scenario. The failure-signature's analogous_contexts explicitly names refund processing as a known variant of this failure class. The structural match across all four required conditions is high. The finding is held at 'candidate' because no behavioral reproduction test has been executed — the outcome of submitting the same refund_reference twice has not been observed at runtime.

proposed_behavioral_test.description: A verification test that exercises the retry scenario against a live instance of process_refund(). The test submits the same refund_reference twice and asserts that exactly one record exists in refund_records afterward. If the assertion fails with count=2, the structural candidate is behaviorally confirmed.
preconditions: Call refund_processor.initialise(db_path=':memory:') to start with an empty store.
steps: Step 1: Call process_refund('REF-RETRY-001', 'ACC-TEST', 19.99) — simulates original submission.
Step 2: Call process_refund('REF-RETRY-001', 'ACC-TEST', 19.99) again — simulates client retry with identical refund_reference.
Step 3: Call get_refunds() and count the returned records.
proposed_behavioral_test.failure_indicator: If get_refunds() returns 2 records, the retry was not deduplicated. This confirms the behavioral pattern: one logical refund produced two durable effects.
proposed_behavioral_test.invariant_being_tested: One logical refund, identified by a unique refund_reference, must produce exactly one record in refund_records regardless of how many times it is submitted.
proposed_behavioral_test.note: This test must NOT be created yet. It is described here as input to the verification stage only.

findings.confidence_rationale: All four required structural conditions from the failure signature are present with direct code-level evidence. The domain (refund processing) is explicitly listed as a known variant in the failure signature. The only uncertainty is behavioral: no test has been run. Confidence in the structural match is high; confirmation awaits the verification stage.
limitations: This finding is based on static code analysis only. No behavioral test has been executed against demo/current/refund_processor.py.
The finding status MUST remain 'candidate' until a behavioral reproduction test in the verification stage confirms that two calls with the same refund_reference produce two refund_records rows.

The module uses an in-memory SQLite database by default. The retry scenario must be tested within a single process session to observe the duplicate, as :memory: databases do not persist across process restarts.
Concurrent call scenarios (two simultaneous submissions of the same refund_reference) are not addressed by this analysis and are not covered by the proposed test.

The failure-signature was extracted from a single synthetic demonstration case. This is the second application of the pattern, but it has not yet been validated across additional independent incidents beyond this one.
unresolved_questions: Will a behavioral test against the current code confirm count=2 for a retried refund_reference, or is there some runtime guard not visible in the static source?

Should a deduplicated retry return the original record silently, or return a distinct 'already processed' response? The historical fix chose silent absorption; the appropriate contract for refunds may differ.
How long should a refund_reference remain active as a deduplication key? The historical fix never expired entries; for long-lived refund systems this may be impractical.
Is there an upstream caller or API layer (not present in this repository) that provides deduplication before reaching process_refund()? If so, the structural risk may be mitigated externally.
